---
title: "Court Surfaces"
editor: visual
---

ATP tournaments are played on three main different surfaces: hard court, clay (green and red), and grass. Specific players often perform better on certain surfaces, because of their game style, the way they grew up, and the types of conditions that they are accustomed to. Most players grow up playing on hard courts, as these are the most plentiful around the world. Certain countries, like Spain, train their players on red clay from the start, which is a surface in which the ball bounces higher and rewards topspin. Finally, grass courts are the rarest surface, yet they carry a rich tradition and tournaments on this surface are considered extremely prestigious. This surface rewards an aggressive playing style, with slices, dropshots, and netplay often utilized.

We are familiar with certain player narratives, such as Nadal dominating on the clay and Federer being the king of grass, and we wanted to see if the data confirmed this.


```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
cleaned_rankings_data <- readRDS(file = here::here("data", "processed", "cleaned_rankings_data.rds"))
atp_singles_data <- readRDS(file = here::here("data", "processed", "atp_singles.Rds"))
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
source(here::here("majorsurface.R"))
```

This first visualization shows the number of titles each player has won on each surface. In comparison to the other players, it is clear that Nadal has won the majority of clay court tournaments. Being from Spain, Nadal has grown up on this surface and has developed a game style that maximizes its advantages. He thrives on long rallies, a high bouncing topsin forehand, and superior movement. His nickname, the "King of Clay," is strongly supported by the data. Additionally, it is shown that Federer has won the most grass court tournaments out of everyone. Federer has traditionally been a serve-and-volleyer, coming to the net and finishing points quickly. This, along with his deadly slice backhand, has made him especially effective on this surface.


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: " "
#| fig.align: "center" 
#| out.width: "800px"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "surfacetitles.png"))
```

The next visualization investigates the percentage of singles matches won on each surface. It is interesting to note that the data confirms aforementioned narratives such as the notion that Nadal plays much better on clay. Nadal and Sinner have clear surfaces they win more on. It is also interesting to note that some players perform relatively poorly on specific surfaces compared to others, with some examples being Alcaraz clearly performing worse on hard surfaces and Federer playing worse on clay. This visualization effectively shows each player's objectively best and worst, as well as likely their favorite and least favorite, surfaces to play on.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: " "
#| fig.align: "center" 
#| out.width: "800px"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "surfacewinp.png"))
```
